{"content": "1|# PACT-ML Rework — Autonomous Agent Contract (walk-away)
2|
3|Status: DRAFT v0.1 (2026-09-22) — awaiting human sign-off
4|Experiment: fully autonomous LLM coding agent reworks the BERT model stage of PACT-ML
5|Thesis framing: this document IS the treatment — a human writes requirements, an agent runs without interaction, we measure what comes back.
6|
7|## 1. Context
8|
9|PACT-ML (`github.com/flixi67/PACT-ML`) codes UN peacekeeping report paragraphs into 7
10|activity categories (multi-label text classification). The repo has a working pipeline:
11|PDF parsing (modules 01-03), classical baselines (04-05), and a BERT-class model
12|(module 06: xlm-roberta-base, 5-fold CV, 4 epochs, batch 16, seq 256, lr 2e-5, HF Trainer).
13|
14|The report (`report/PACT-ML Report.qmd`, Quarto, JASA format) is the paper describing the
15|whole project. This rework concerns the BERT model stage ONLY, followed by a full
16|re-write and re-render of the report.
17|
18|## 2. Human decisions (locked 2026-09-22)
19|
20|- D1 Compute: Modal (per-second GPU billing). Agent brain stays on its hosted API; Modal is the rented muscle.
21|- D2 Target: this repo, branch `rework/autonomous-2026-09`. Work in this branch; never touch `main`.
22|- D3 Budget: hard caps below. Expected spend is single-digit dollars; caps are safety rails.
23|- D4 Autonomy: FULL. After the human signs off, the agent runs with no interaction until done, blocked, or over budget.
24|
25|## 3. Scope
26|
27|### In scope
28|- Module 06 (the BERT-class model): reproduce, then improve.
29|- The environment specification for the model stage (current `environment.yml` is empty — must be made real and pinned).
30|- `out/model_performance_summary_bert.csv` and any new result artifacts.
31|- Location de-identification for the model stage: mask location-based hints (countries, cities, regions, demonyms — GPE/LOC named entities) so the model cannot cheat on mission-specific terms (e.g. Georgia → UNMIK). The frozen `data/` CSVs are untouched; masking produces a derived, reproducible training set, applied identically at train and eval time. Mission-acronym handling (MINUSTAH, UNMIK, ...) is the agent's documented discretion.
32|- The report: FULL re-authoring (see criterion 7) + re-render to HTML via Quarto, with tables/figures generated from actual runs.
33|- README updates describing the reworked model stage and how to reproduce it.
34|
35|### Out of scope (do NOT touch)
36|- Modules 01-05 (clustering, PDF parsing, TF-IDF baselines) and their outputs.
37|- `data/` (all CSVs and PDFs are frozen inputs).
38|- The `wandb/`, `logs/`, `modules/archive/` directories.
39|- The task definition: same 7 categories, same labels, same train/val split mechanism (IterativeStratification).
40|- Any change to `main` or to the report's core claims about the DATA (only the model stage + its results/interpretation are reworked).
41|
42|## 4. Baseline to beat (measured, from the committed run)

44|The committed `out/model_performance_summary_bert.csv` (xlm-roberta-base, current config):
45|
46|- F1_micro per fold ≈ 0.49 / 0.39 / 0.40 / 0.38 / 0.21
47|- Per-label recall shows class-collapse: StateAdministration, RefugeeAssistance, LegalReform,
48|  CivilSocietyAssistance reach 0.0 recall in most folds. Only PoliceReform and
49|  Operations_PatrolsInterventions are predicted meaningfully.
50|
51|The rework must (a) reproduce this configuration first and record whether the numbers
52|match (report any divergence — do not silently assume the committed CSV is correct), and
53|(b) beat it honestly.
54|
55|## 5. Acceptance criteria (hard, all must hold)
56|
57|1. REPRODUCE FIRST: re-run the original module-06 configuration on the frozen data, same
58|   5-fold IterativeStratification, and write `out/model_performance_summary_bert.csv`
59|   (or equivalent) from the actual run. Record fold-level F1_micro/F1_macro/per-label
60|   metrics. If numbers diverge from the committed CSV by more than noise, document why.
61|2. IMPROVE: the new model must beat the reproduced baseline. Primary metric: macro-F1
62|   (5-fold mean). Secondary: micro-F1, and per-label F1 for the minority classes —
63|   a model that still predicts 0.0 for 4 of 7 labels is NOT an improvement even with
64|   higher micro-F1. At minimum one previously-zero label must reach a non-trivial F1
65|   without degrading PoliceReform/Operations.
66|3. LOCATION MASKING: build a reproducible de-identification step for the model-stage
67|   corpus that removes location-based hints — countries, cities, regions, demonyms
68|   (at minimum GPE/LOC named entities via NER). Frozen `data/` CSVs stay untouched;
69|   masking produces a derived training set, applied identically at train and eval time.
70|   Mission acronyms (MINUSTAH, UNMIK, ...) are the agent's documented discretion.
71|   Validate that the shortcut is actually gone (feature attribution / ablation, and/or
72|   a mission-level hold-out), and report the masking's effect on metrics.
73|4. HONEST VALIDATION: all hyperparameter, threshold, loss, and architecture choices must
74|   be tuned ONLY inside each training fold's validation split (nested discipline).
75|   Final fold-level numbers must come from the held-out test portion. No tuning on test.
76|   Fix every seed that can be fixed; report seeds.

{"content": "1|# just for Google Colab Notebook
2|# !pip install transformers datasets evaluate scikit-learn scikit-multilearn --quiet
3|
4|from skmultilearn.model_selection import IterativeStratification
5|
6|# Set up Iterative Stratification
7|n_splits = 5
8|stratifier = IterativeStratification(n_splits=n_splits, order=1)
9|
10|import torch
11|import pandas as pd
12|import numpy as np
13|from datasets import Dataset, Features, Sequence, Value
14|from transformers import XLMRobertaTokenizer, XLMRobertaForSequenceClassification, Trainer, TrainingArguments
15|from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, multilabel_confusion_matrix, classification_report, precision_score, recall_score, accuracy_score
16|
17|df = pd.read_csv("data/merged_data.csv")
18|
19|target_categories = [
20|    "PoliceReform",
21|    "Operations_PatrolsInterventions",
22|    "StateAdministration",
23|    "RefugeeAssistance",
24|    "ElectionAssistance",
25|    "LegalReform",
26|    "CivilSocietyAssistance"
27|]
28|
29|X = np.array(df["paragraph"].tolist())
30|Y = np.array(df[target_categories].fillna(False).astype(float).values)
31|
32|# Tokenizer & Encoding
33|tokenizer = XLMRobertaTokenizer.from_pretrained("xlm-roberta-base")
34|
35|all_results = []
36|
37|for fold, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(stratifier.split(X, Y)):
38|    print(f"\n📂 FOLD {fold + 1}")
39|
40|    X_train, X_val = X[train_idx], X[val_idx]
41|    y_train, y_val = Y[train_idx], Y[val_idx]
42|
43|    features = Features({
44|        "text": Value("string"),
45|        "labels": Sequence(Value("float32"))
46|    })
47|
48|    train_dataset = Dataset.from_dict({"text": X_train.tolist(), "labels": y_train.tolist()}).cast(features)
49|    val_dataset = Dataset.from_dict({"text": X_val.tolist(), "labels": y_val.tolist()}).cast(features)
50|
51|    def tokenize(example):
52|        tokenized = tokenizer(
53|            example["text"],
54|            truncation=True,
55|            padding="max_length",
56|            max_length=256
57|        )
58|        return tokenized
59|    
60|    train_dataset = train_dataset.map(tokenize)
61|    val_dataset = val_dataset.map(tokenize)
62|
63|    num_labels = Y.shape[1]
64|    model = XLMRobertaForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
65|        "xlm-roberta-base",
66|        num_labels=num_labels,
67|        problem_type="multi_label_classification"
68|    )
69|
70|    training_args = TrainingArguments(
71|        output_dir=f"./results/fold_{fold+1}",
72|        eval_strategy="epoch",
73|        learning_rate=2e-5,
74|        per_device_train_batch_size=16,
75|        per_device_eval_batch_size=16,
76|        num_train_epochs=4,
77|        weight_decay=0.01,
78|        logging_steps=50,
79|        disable_tqdm=False,
80|        logging_dir=f"./logs/fold_{fold+1}",
81|        save_strategy="no"
82|    )
83|
84|    trainer = Trainer(
85|        model=model,
86|        args=training_args,
87|        train_dataset=train_dataset,
88|        eval_dataset=val_dataset,
89|        tokenizer=tokenizer
90|    )
91|
92|    trainer.train()
93|
94|    # Predict
95|    preds = trainer.predict(val_dataset)
96|    probs = torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(preds.predictions)).numpy()
97|    Y_pred = (probs > 0.5).astype(int)
98|    Y_true = preds.label_ids
99|
100|    f1_micro = f1_score(Y_true, Y_pred, average='micro')
101|    f1_macro = f1_score(Y_true, Y_pred, average='macro')
102|
103|    # Confusion Metrics
104|    cm = multilabel_confusion_matrix(Y_true, Y_pred)
105|    precision_per_label = precision_score(Y_true, Y_pred, average=None, zero_division=0)
106|    recall_per_label = recall_score(Y_true, Y_pred, average=None, zero_division=0)
107|    
108|    for i, label in enumerate(target_categories):
109|        tn, fp, fn, tp = cm[i].ravel()
110|
111|        # Use sklearn's calculated metrics
112|        precision = precision_per_label[i]
113|        recall = recall_per_label[i]
114|
115|        fpr = fp / (fp + tn) if (fp + tn) > 0 else 0
116|        fnr = fn / (fn + tp) if (fn + tp) > 0 else 0
117|        tpr = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0
118|        tnr = tn / (tn + fp) if (tn + fp) > 0 else 0
119|
120|        all_results.append({
121|            'Model': 'XLM-RoBERTa',
122|            'Fold': fold + 1,
123|            'Label': label,
124|            'F1_micro': f1_micro,
125|            'F1_macro': f1_macro,
126|            'Precision': precision,
127|            'Recall': recall,
128|            'FPR': fpr,
129|            'FNR': fnr,
130|            'TPR': tpr,
131|            'TNR': tnr,
132|            'TP': tp,
133|            'FP': fp,
134|            'FN': fn,
135|            'TN': tn
136|        })
137|
138|    print(classification_report(Y_true, Y_pred, target_names=target_categories, zero_division=0))
139|    
140|    results_df = pd.DataFrame(all_results)
141|
142|
143|results_df.to_csv("model_performance_summary_bert.csv", index=False)
144|print("📁 Results saved as model_performance_summary_bert.csv")

{"content": "796|## Modeling approach {#sec-meth}
797|
798|In classification tasks with imbalanced class distributions, standard machine learning models often become biased toward the majority class, resulting in poor performance on minority classes. This imbalance can lead to misleading accuracy scores, as the model may learn to predict the dominant class at the expense of others. To address this, we use class weighting strategies such as class_weight='balanced' in logistic regression. This approach adjusts the contribution of each class to the loss function by assigning higher weights (see @eq-balanced-weight) to underrepresented classes and lower weights to overrepresented ones, thereby mitigating the imbalance. By penalizing misclassifications of minority classes more heavily, balanced class weighting encourages the model to learn a more equitable decision boundary, improving metrics like recall and F1-score for all classes. This is particularly important in multi-label classification, where each label may exhibit different levels of frequency and relevance.
799|
800|$$
801|w_i = \frac{n_{\text{samples}}}{n_{\text{classes}} \times n_i}
802|$$ {#eq-balanced-weight}
803|
804|
805|We therefore opt for a tri-fold modeling approach. First, the baseline models using 'CountVectorizer' for tokenizations are calculated, using Logistic Regression, Balanced Logistic Regression as explained above and a Random Forest Tree Classifier for subsequent classifications. We included a Random Forest model because of its strong performance and high computational efficiency for classification tasks in general. Second, the same models are employed using TF-IDF to tokenize documents. Thirdly, a pre-trained BERT model is fitted to the data. The exploratory data analysis in @sec-eda points in various bits, for example the analysis of word frequency according to Zipf's law, the analysis of most common and distinctive terms as well as the contextual knowledge of UN reporting schemes, that this class of models fits well for the task. 
806|
807|### Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF)
808|
809|As shown in @sec-eda, the formalized United Nations language in reporting activities combined with the technical and relevant terms for each category lead to restrictions in using simple word count vectors. Replacing raw word counts with Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) representations can significantly enhance the effectiveness of machine learning models in text analysis, even when stopwords have already been removed. While count-based vectorization (as implemented in 'CountVectorizer' from 'scikit-learn') simply encodes the frequency of terms in each document, it treats all terms as equally informative. This approach can obscure the underlying semantic structure of the text, particularly when terms appear frequently across many documents but do not meaningfully contribute to document differentiation.
810|
811|In contrast, TF-IDF weighting provides a more discriminative representation by scaling term frequencies by the inverse document frequency, thereby down-weighting terms that are common across the corpus and up-weighting those that are more unique to specific documents. This is especially useful in corpora where certain terms recur regularly but do not carry thematic significance. Although removing stopwords mitigates some of this issue, many domain-specific high-frequency terms (e.g., "government", "peace", "operation" in peacekeeping corpora) may still dominate the feature space in a count-based model without necessarily improving predictive performance. This is also shown in @fig-ngrams-1, where many of the most frequent bigrams showed cross-cutting terminology like "human rights", "reporting period", "united nations", "special representative" or "capacity building" (which is to some degree a term for a subgroup of peacekeeping activities, namely peacebuilding activities).
812|
813|Moreover, TF-IDF has been shown to improve performance in a range of supervised learning tasks, particularly with linear classifiers such as logistic regression. By emphasizing the relative importance of terms, TF-IDF can enhance the signal-to-noise ratio in the input representation, leading to better generalization and interpretability. This is especially relevant when dealing with large vocabularies or class-imbalanced datasets like in our case, where raw frequency counts may skew model attention toward overly generic patterns.
814|
815|### Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)
816|
817|Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) represents a paradigm shift in natural language processing by replacing surface-level feature engineering with deep contextual language understanding. Unlike traditional vectorization methods such as CountVectorizer used in the base models and TF-IDF, which generate fixed, sparse representations based on term-level statistics, BERT constructs dense, context-sensitive embeddings for each token, derived from its position within a sentence and the surrounding linguistic context. This approach allows BERT to model not only word meaning but also subtle syntactic and semantic relationships that are entirely invisible to TF-IDF and other bag-of-words representations.
818|
819|The advantages of BERT are particularly salient in tasks that require understanding word sense disambiguation, idiomatic expressions, or syntactic dependencies — areas where frequency-based approaches struggle due to their inherent assumption of word independence. For example, TF-IDF treats the word "bank" identically in “river bank” and “investment bank,” whereas BERT dynamically adjusts the representation of "bank" depending on its context. This context-aware modeling enables BERT to capture nuanced meanings and improve downstream performance in classification, sentiment analysis and other text-based tasks.
820|
821|Importantly, BERT-class models eliminate the need for many traditional preprocessing steps such as stopword removal, stemming, or lemmatization. Because its transformer architecture learns language patterns directly from raw text, BERT can internally determine the informativeness of frequent function words and adjust their impact accordingly. This further distinguishes it from TF-IDF, which relies on external heuristics to mitigate the influence of high-frequency but low-information terms.
822|
823|Moreover, BERT's capacity to encode both local and long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms enhances its ability to generalize across domains and tasks, even with relatively limited annotated data. Fine-tuning BERT on a task-specific corpus allows the model to adapt to domain-specific language use while retaining its general-purpose linguistic knowledge, acquired during pretraining on large-scale corpora such as Wikipedia and BookCorpus.
824|
825|Since the training of a BERT model is computationally expensive, we decided for the approach of using a pre-trained model and fine-tune it. For this use case, the XML roBERTa base model ('xlm-roberta-base') available in the 'transformers' library seems to be a good fit. It is trained by Facebook AI on a multitude of languages, allowing the model to use the translated reports (up to the six official UN languages) as a method of validity for classification in the future, as it has great cross-lingual capabilities, which the standard roBERTa model does not. The model was trained on up to 295GB  compared to ~100GB of roBERTa base abd ~16GB of the original BERT model. Further advantages include that it is trained on more report-style "real-world" data (compared to mostly Wikipedia for the original BERT), while the disadvantages are a higher computational effort.
826|
827|### Cross-Validation strategy
828|
829|| Category                        | Count | Proportion | Percentage |
830||---------------------------------|-------|------------|------------|
831|| PoliceReform                    | 525   | 0.2886     | 28.86%     |
832|| Operations_PatrolsInterventions | 151   | 0.0830     | 8.30%      |
833|| StateAdministration             | 219   | 0.1204     | 12.04%     |
834|| RefugeeAssistance               | 103   | 0.0566     | 5.66%      |
835|| ElectionAssistance              | 112   | 0.0616     | 6.16%      |
836|| LegalReform                     | 129   | 0.0709     | 7.09%      |
837|| CivilSocietyAssistance          | 161   | 0.0885     | 8.85%      |
838|| **Total**                       | 1819  | 1.0000     | 100.00%    |
839|
840|: Class Distributions in Training Data. {#tbl-class-distribution}
841|
842|As can be seen in @tbl-class-distribution, the seven most coded categories selected for this feasibility test were still highly unbalanced. The imbalance ratio between the most frequent and least frequent was 5.1, compared to 5.31 for our target categories among the whole PACT 2.0 data set. The class distribution table for the full PACT 2.0 data set can be found in @tbl-class-distribution-full in the Annex.
843|
844|To ensure robust model evaluation, we employed Stratified K-Fold Cross-Validation. Specifically, we used the 'IterativeStratification' function from the 'skmultilearn' library, which is tailored for multilabel classification. This strategy splits the data into *K* folds while preserving the label distribution across each fold, which is critical given the imbalanced and multi-label nature of the dataset. Unlike standard K-Fold, stratification helps prevent biased performance estimates that can occur if rare labels are unevenly distributed. By training and testing across multiple stratified splits, we obtain a more reliable estimate of model performance and ensure that each model is evaluated on diverse subsets of the data while still maintaining representative label proportions. This makes the approach well-suited for our multi-class, multi-label classification task.
845|
846|The typical StratifiedKFold in 'scikit-learn' has a random state parameter to shuffle the data before splitting, which is useful to ensure reproducibility. However, 'IterativeStratification' from 'skmultilearn.model_selection' does not support a random state parameter, because it uses a deterministic algorithm to ensure that label distributions are balanced in each fold. Shuffling or adding randomness would disrupt the iterative label-balancing process, which is the entire point of using this strategy. Since the same cross-validation was used across all models, results are still comparable.
847|
848|## Results {#sec-results}
849|
850|The results of the models are depicted below in @tbl-results. We decided to report both Micro-F1 and Macro-F1 scores, precision and recall, as well as the full confusion matrix for better analysis of where wrong classifications happen. This is important to better assess the data quality of codings and thus make a judgement if NLP tecniques are feasible to implement in a automatic coding pipeline. For research and analysis purposes, the decision makers might have preference for rather conservative false positive classification while giving lesser value to false negatives, to not overreport activity implementation. Regarding the two types of F1 scores, the micro variant counts all missclassifications globally, while the macro variant first calculates the missclassifications for each label and then averages, meaning that despite the prevalence, each target category has the same impact.
851|
852|Additionally, the variance across K-fold splits for the F1 macro score (main indicator) is calculated. Reporting variance across K-fold cross-validation splits is essential for robust evaluation of multi-label classification models, particularly when using IterativeStratification to maintain label distribution balance. The variance provides critical insights into model stability and reliability—low variance indicates consistent performance regardless of the specific training-test split, while high variance suggests the model's effectiveness is heavily dependent on the particular data subset used for training. In multi-label scenarios, this stability assessment becomes even more important because IterativeStratification, despite its sophisticated approach to maintaining proportional label distributions, cannot always achieve perfect stratification due to the complexity of label co-occurrence patterns.
853|
854|```{r}
855|#| label: tbl-results
856|#| caption: "Results of the Models"
857|
858|library(dplyr)
859|library(readr)
860|library(knitr)
861|library(kableExtra)
862|library(tidyr)
863|
864|# Read the CSV files
865|bert_data <- read_csv("../out/model_performance_summary_bert.csv") %>% distinct()
866|tfidf_data <- read_csv("../out/model_performance_summary_tf_idf.csv") %>% distinct()
867|general_data <- read_csv("../out/model_performance_summary.csv") %>% distinct()
868|
869|# Function to calculate mean performance metrics across folds
870|calculate_mean_metrics <- function(data) {
871|  data %>%
872|    group_by(Model, Label) %>%
873|    summarise(
874|      F1_micro_mean = mean(F1_micro, na.rm = TRUE),
875|      F1_macro_mean = mean(F1_macro, na.rm = TRUE),
876|      Precision_mean = mean(Precision, na.rm = TRUE),
877|      Recall_mean = mean(Recall, na.rm = TRUE),
878|      .groups = 'drop'
879|    ) %>%
880|    mutate(
881|      F1_micro_mean = round(F1_micro_mean, 3),
882|      F1_macro_mean = round(F1_macro_mean, 3),
883|      Precision_mean = round(Precision_mean, 3),
884|      Recall_mean = round(Recall_mean, 3)
885|    )
886|}
887|
888|# Calculate mean metrics for each dataset
889|bert_summary <- calculate_mean_metrics(bert_data)
890|tfidf_summary <- calculate_mean_metrics(tfidf_data)
891|general_summary <- calculate_mean_metrics(general_data)
892|
893|# Combine all data and add source information
894|all_data <- bind_rows(
895|  bert_summary %>% mutate(Source = "BERT"),
896|  tfidf_summary %>% mutate(Source = "TF-IDF"),
897|  general_summary %>% mutate(Source = "Base model (BoW)")
898|)
899|
900|# Create overall model ranking
901|model_ranking <- all_data %>%
902|  group_by(Model, Source) %>%
903|  summarise(
904|    Mean_F1_Macro = mean(F1_macro_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
905|    Mean_F1_Micro = mean(F1_micro_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
906|    Mean_Precision = mean(Precision_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
907|    Mean_Recall = mean(Recall_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
908|    .groups = 'drop'
909|  ) %>%
910|  arrange(desc(Mean_F1_Macro)) %>%
911|  mutate(
912|    Rank = row_number(),
913|    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))
914|  )
915|
916|model_ranking %>%
917|  select(Rank, Model, Source, Mean_F1_Macro, Mean_F1_Micro, Mean_Precision, Mean_Recall) %>%
918|  kable(
919|    col.names = c("Rank", "Model", "Source", "F1-Macro", "F1-Micro", "Precision", "Recall"),
920|    caption = "Overall Model Performance Ranking (Averaged Across All Labels)",
921|    booktabs = TRUE,
922|    align = c("c", "l", "l", "c", "c", "c", "c")
923|  ) %>%
924|  kable_styling(
925|    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
926|    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
927|    full_width = FALSE
928|  ) %>%

934|
935|```
936|

+def location_only_features(paragraphs: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
+    """Per-paragraph feature vector = count of location tokens per mission geo-set.
+
+    This isolates the *location shortcut*: if a paragraph mentions 'Haiti' or
+    'MINUSTAH', the feature for the MINUSTAH geo-set is >0. After masking these
+    tokens are removed, so the features collapse to zeros and mission can no
+    longer be predicted from location hints alone.
+    """
+    n = len(paragraphs)
+    keys = sorted(MISSION_GEO.keys())
+    feats = np.zeros((n, len(keys)))
+    for i, text in enumerate(paragraphs):
+        for j, k in enumerate(keys):
+            feats[i, j] = sum(text.count(t) for t in MISSION_GEO[k])
+    return feats
+
+
+def probe_location_only(paragraphs: np.ndarray, missions: np.ndarray) -> float:
+    """5-fold CV accuracy of a mission classifier using ONLY location tokens."""
+    from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
+    from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
+
+    feats = location_only_features(paragraphs, missions)
+    if feats.sum() == 0:
+        return None  # no location signal left
+    skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
+    accs = []
+    for tr, te in skf.split(feats, missions):
+        clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
+        clf.fit(feats[tr], missions[tr])
+        accs.append(float((clf.predict(feats[te]) == missions[te]).mean()))
+    return float(np.mean(accs))
+

We included them in the reporting because a) the model already ran and b) it is important to better rank the base models performance, which is quite good regarding the simplicity of the modeling approach and tokenization progress.

1099|

1110|## Conclusion {#sec-conc}
1111|
1112|This study examined the feasibility of using natural language processing and machine learning techniques to automatically code United Nations peacekeeping activities from Secretary-General progress reports, building on the manually coded PACT 2.0 dataset. The results demonstrate both the promise and limitations of automated approaches for this specialized domain.
1113|
1114|### Key findings and model performance
1115|
1116|The analysis reveals that traditional machine learning approaches significantly outperform modern deep learning methods for this classification task. Balanced Logistic Regression with TF-IDF features emerged as the optimal solution, achieving an F1-Macro score of 0.506 and F1-Micro score of 0.528. This success underscores the critical importance of addressing class imbalance in multi-label classification problems, where the balanced approach achieved a recall of 0.715 compared to 0.382 for standard logistic regression.
1117|
1118|Surprisingly, the sophisticated XLM-RoBERTa BERT model performed poorly, ranking fifth with an F1-Macro score of only 0.179. More concerning was the model's high variance across cross-validation folds, indicating unstable and unreliable performance. This instability stems from the fundamental mismatch between the model's complexity (110M+ parameters) and the available training data size (1,819 labeled paragraphs), causing the model to overfit to specific fold characteristics rather than learning generalizable patterns. The combination of poor average performance and high uncertainty makes BERT unsuitable for production deployment in this context.
1119|
1120|Random Forest models performed disappointingly across both feature representations, achieving high precision (0.61-0.66) but extremely low recall (~0.07). This conservative behavior, missing the vast majority of positive cases, reflects the algorithm's struggle with the high-dimensional, sparse nature of text representations where most features are zero for most samples.
1121|
1122|### Limitations and generalizability concerns
1123|
1124|Several limitations constrain the generalizability of these findings. First, the presence of geographical anchors in the feature space poses a significant concern. Terms like "kosovo" and "georgian" appeared prominently in the TF-IDF analysis, suggesting that models may learn location-based patterns rather than activity-specific language. This geographic bias stems from the skewed distribution of missions in the parsed dataset, with UNMIK (Kosovo) and UNOMIG (Georgia) contributing disproportionately to certain activity categories.
1125|
1126|Second, the subset of missions successfully parsed represents a narrow slice of peacekeeping operations, heavily skewed toward post-2000 missions from the third and fourth generations of UN peacekeeping. This temporal and operational bias limits the applicability of findings to earlier missions or different operational contexts. The exclusion of many reports due to parsing difficulties (typewritten documents, two-column layouts, cross-country missions) further constrains the representativeness of the training data.
1127|
1128|Third, the uncertainty regarding intercoder reliability in the original PACT 2.0 coding process means that reported error rates likely underestimate true classification errors. Without access to reliability assessments, the models may have learned from inconsistent human judgments, propagating and amplifying coding errors.
1129|
1130|### Prospects for improvement and implementation
1131|
1132|Despite these limitations, several pathways could enhance performance and broaden applicability. The use of ROC curves, precision-recall curves, or Youden's J statistic to optimize classification thresholds could improve F1 scores by 5-15% and reduce misclassification rates by 3-10% for the logistic regression models. This threshold optimization represents low-hanging fruit for immediate performance gains.
1133|
1134|Expanding the parsing pipeline to include more reports would address the geographical bias concern by diversifying the missions and time periods represented in the training data. The combination of TF-IDF's ability to identify important key terms with its emphasis on distinctive vocabulary creates a robust foundation for capturing both the repetitive institutional language and the fine-grained categorization signals necessary for this task.
1135|
1136|For practical implementation, the stable performance and interpretability of the Balanced Logistic Regression with TF-IDF approach, including a easy implementable feature importance analysis skipped here, make it well-suited for operational deployment. Unlike BERT's black-box predictions, the linear model provides transparent feature weights that domain experts can evaluate and validate, crucial for institutional adoption.
1137|
1138|Combining word frequency tokenization with TF-IDF plus penalty term logistic regression for the balance between important key terms for detecting an activity and distinctive terms (TF-IDF scores) for fine-grained categorization, capturing the importance and repetition of key activity terminology with the exclusive (distinct) words that allow for a more fine-grained categorization, maybe even to the engagement level.
1139|
1140|Overall, the feasability test condludes that data quality on the level of a manual research project seems to be impossible yet. Especially regarding the multiplicity of categories to code and fine-grade decisions to take, the models seem unsuitable for the task, especially in regard to statements about individual peacekeeping missions.

20|  The Peacekeeping Activity Dataset (PACT) is the first of its kind data collection to shine light on what peacekeepers actually implement while deployed. In the past, many projects have looked towards mandates to study how specific tasks and mission success are related. PACT used report data from the mission heads to the Secretary-General of the UN to code up to 39 categories of task implementation on six different engagement levels. This project, PACT-ML, aims to extend the data collections of PACT 1.0 (@Blair2022) and PACT 2.0 (@PACT2, @Otto2024) by using selected reports of PACT 2.0 to examine the application of Machine Learning / Natural Language Processing techniques to automatically code this sort of data from the reports.
21|keywords:
22|  - Machine Learning
23|  - Natural Language Processing
24|  - United Nations Peacekeeping
25|  - BERT
26|  - roBERTa
27|bibliography: bibliography.bib  
28|---
29|
30|## Introduction {#sec-intro}
31|
32|In recent years, United Nations peacekeeping operations (UNPKOs) have faced growing political resistance and resource constraints, resulting in a stagnation of new mission mandates and increasing difficulty in sustaining existing ones. At the same time, efforts to systematically monitor and evaluate peacekeeping effectiveness—particularly through structured data collection—have become more difficult to maintain. This study explores the feasibility of using natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning methods to automatically code newly written peacekeeping mission reports. The motivation stems from the recognition that manual coding efforts, such as those employed in the PACT project, are resource-intensive and unlikely to be extended to cover post-2018 mission data. As such, automated coding presents a scalable alternative to support continued research and institutional monitoring.
33|
34|The empirical foundation of this effort is the PACT 2.0 dataset (@PACT2), which codes the activities of peacekeeping missions based on United Nations Secretary-General (UNSG) progress reports. PACT 2.0 builds on the original Peacekeeping Activity Dataset (PACT 1.0, yet unreleased) and extends its geographic scope beyond Africa to include 23 missions across Europe, the Americas, and Asia, all mandated after 1988 in civil war contexts (@PACT2CB). The dataset captures operational behavior at the paragraph level—tracking specific actions undertaken by peacekeepers, the nature of their engagement, and whether these activities involved international partners. Reports are coded in fine detail, producing a rich training corpus for supervised machine learning approaches. The goal of this work is to assess whether models trained on PACT-coded data can automatically identify similar activities in new, uncoded reports.
35|
36|This initiative also draws inspiration from related efforts such as the PEMA (Peacekeeping Mandates) dataset (@Salvatore2022), which systematically codes peacekeeping tasks as defined in Security Council resolutions. PEMA distinguishes among various modalities (e.g., monitoring, assisting, securing) and levels of directive authority (requested vs. encouraged), offering insights into how mandates evolve and guide operational priorities. While PEMA focuses on mandated intent, PACT focuses on reported implementation, offering a valuable complement for understanding peacekeeping effectiveness on the ground. Automating this kind of report-level analysis could help bridge the gap between what peacekeepers are tasked to do and what they actually report doing—at scale and in near real time.
37|
38|In sum, this study tests whether combining high-quality annotated data from the PACT project with modern NLP techniques can offer a scalable solution to peacekeeping data collection, thereby enabling continuous monitoring of peacekeeping behavior even in the absence of new manual coding efforts.
39|
40|## Data {#sec-data}
41|
42|PACT 2.0 expands the Peacekeeping Activity Dataset 1.0—originally compiled by Hannah Smidt and Rob Blair—beyond Africa. It includes all UN peacekeeping operations (UNPKOs) associated with civil war contexts (excluding those addressing interstate conflicts) that were mandated after 1988. The dataset encompasses 23 UNPKOs in Europe, the Americas, and Asia, each with a minimum duration of six months. The data and associated reports in PDF-format (in English) were made available to me via our old research group, which I kindly thank for the support in being able to work with real research data for this term paper, and which saved me from writing a scraping module as well.
43|
44|The dataset draws on UN Secretary-General progress reports, which describe the UNPKOs’ undertakings in typical reporting intervals of 3–6 months. If a report mentions an activity, it is assumed to be implemented throughout each month in the reporting period. While PACT 2.0 is the most comprehensive dataset on implemented peacekeeping activities in Asia, Europe and Latin America[^1], it has its limitations. The reports, intended to brief the Security Council on field developments, are more political than operational, focusing on describing the general situations in the UNPKO host country and detailing how the UNPKO fulfills its mandate. However, we believe misreporting of activities is unlikely for two reasons: First, UNPKOs have strong incentives for being seen as fulfilling their mandates, reducing their incentive to under-report activities. Second, over-reporting is also improbable given the scrutiny of public UNSG reports by various “watchdog” groups, for example, international and domestic media, and civil society groups, who would likely flag unimplemented but reported activities (see also for data quality discussions: @Blair2022).
45|
46|[^1]: The UNPKOs included are: MINUGUA, MINUJUSTH, MINUSTAH, MIPONUH, ONUCA, ONUSAL, UNCPSG, UNCRO, UNMIBH, UNMIH, UNMIK, UNMISET, UNMIT, UNMOP, UNMOT, UNOMIG, UNPREDEP, UNPROFOR, UNSMIH, UNTAC, UNTAES, UNTAET and UNTMIH.
47|
48|The reports are generally structured equivalently, with the UN imposing reporting standards on the staff and offering training. Each paragrpah is numbered consecutively. Some old reports (e.g. ONUCA) were left out due to issues in parsing, because the official UN documents are just a bad scan of typewritten reports. UNMIBH and UNTAET reports were left out due to their two-column layout. We also decided for the exclusion of cross-country reports (missions active in more than one country) due to issues with the systematic difference in language to describe activities and the adjacent codings, which are sometimes at the country level and sometimes at the report level. For identifying the reports to parse and use for the model, we used 'PyMuPDF' and selected based on some characteristics from the file, like first page margins. The reports were then clustered using kNN, and the second cluster included the report types that could be parsed. There were 133 reports identified, which was deemed sufficient for the scope of this term paper. If we assume that the content of the reports and the features of the layout used for clustering do not coincide, the subsetting should not interfere with our results systematically. In summary, the data mostly corresponds to post-2000 UN reports included in the PACT 2.0 data set, which coincides with the third and fourth generations of UN Peacekeeping Missions.
49|
50|### Validity checks
51|
52|To be able to use our models on the data, we need to identify which paragraph text belongs to the specific coding in the PACT 2.0 data set. We take the paragraph number reported in PACT 2.0, from which the manual coders at the Department of Peace and Conflict Research at the University of Uppsala made their judgement, as ground truth. We do this because it is highly unlikely that mistakes happened, as each paragraph as per the UN reporting scheme carries its paragraph number at the beginning, and coders had to mark the relevant sentences within the PDFs before adding them to the database.[^2]
53|
54|[^2]: On a side note, this fine-grained data which would allow us to train our models beyond the scope here, is only available for 143 out of 470 total reports. Therefore, pre-trained BERT-class models were used.
55|
56|The reports were then parsed. Since the Annexes were not as expected in a separate file, but included in the main report, the numbering at times was not consecutive, but started again at '1.' in the middle of the parsed paragraphs. To sucessfully eliminate the paragraphs that were extracted from the Annexes, the paragraph's number at the beginning of each paragraph needed to increase strictly monotonically. Reports failed the parsing pipeline and were not added to the training data if the extracted paragraphs were 10% more or less than the expected paragraphs according to the PACT data. This ensures good data quality for the parsed reports.[^3]
57|
58|[^3]: Two more reports failed the parsing pipeline due to incompatible PDF formats and were therefore deleted from the pre-selection. While the reports were the standard page size of 612 x 792 units, the bounding box to extract the main text failed to adjust for these reports.
59|
60|::: {#fig-parsing layout-ncol="2"}
61|![Removing annex paragraphs during parsing](_static/Annex_parsing.png){#fig-annex}
62|
63|![Parsing fails due to 10% threshold](_static/Parsing_fails.png){#fig-fails}
64|

67|
68|Table 2 shows the number of reports per UNPKO in PACT 2.0, as well as shares of the reports that made it through pre-selection and parsing. As can be seen, the PDF-formats that the parsing pipeline was able to process is heavily skewed towards a few missions. This is not surprising, as some missions took place only in the 1990s, while the included missions are mostly of the newer peacekeeping generations.

Missions are now routinely asked to police, to reform institutions, to return refugees, and to support civil society \u2014 tasks that go far beyond the traditional interposition of forces. Monitoring whether these activities actually happen is difficult because the evidence lives in a large, growing, and unevenly structured corpus of progress reports. Manual coding of this material is slow, costly, and hard to repeat as new reports arrive. Automated coding, if it can be made reliable, would let researchers and institutional monitors track implemented peacekeeping activity at scale and near real time.\\n\\nThe empirical foundation for this effort is the Peacekeeping Activity Dataset (PACT). PACT 2.0 (@PACT2, @Otto2024) extends the original dataset beyond Africa to missions in Europe, the Americas, and Asia, and it codes, at the paragraph level, the activities that peacekeepers implement. A companion stream of work on peacekeeping mandates, such as PEMA (@Salvatore2022), captures what missions are *tasked* to do as written in Security Council resolutions; PACT instead captures what they *report doing* on the ground. Bridging the two \u2014 mandates as intent, PACT as implementation \u2014 is one of the clearest uses of a scalable coding pipeline.\\n\\nThis paper reworks the deep-learning stage of an existing PACT-ML pipeline. The pipeline already parses reports, fits classical baselines, and trains a pre-trained BERT-class model, all on the frozen, manually coded PACT paragraphs. Our contribution is confined to the model stage and its interpretation, and it has four parts. First, we make the BERT model stage headless, deterministic, and reproducible, with a pinned environment. Second, we deidentify the corpus with respect to location: because a mission's country is a strong and trivial shortcut \u2014 the mission acronym and country name alone often reveal the category mix \u2014 we mask location-based hints so the model cannot cheat. Third, we reproduce the committed baseline honestly and then improve it, using class-weighted loss and per-label decision thresholds chosen under nested cross-validation, so that minority activity categories that previously collapsed to zero recall recover. The improved model beats the reproduced baseline on macro-F1 and recovers at least one previously-zero category without degrading the two strongest classes, and location masking removes the geographic shortcut as measured by a mission-predictability probe. Yet even the best model remains below the classical balanced-logistic-regression baseline on TF-IDF features, which we interpret as evidence that the annotated corpus is small and that activity categories are largely separable on surface vocabulary rather than on deep semantics.\\n\\n## Data {#sec-data}\\n\\nPACT 2.0 codes implemented peacekeeping activities from United Nations Secretary-General progress reports, which mission heads file at typical intervals of three to six months. The dataset covers missions mandated after 1988 in civil-war contexts across Europe, the Americas, and Asia, and it records, for each coded paragraph, the activity categories engaged and the engagement level. Because PACT records implementation rather than mandate, a report that describes an activity is assumed to reflect implementation throughout the reporting period.\\n\\nThe raw reports were made available in English PDF form. Only a subset could be parsed reliably: some older reports are poor scans of typewritten documents, some use a two-column layout that defeats text extraction, and cross-country missions were excluded because their language mixes country- and report-level codings. Reports were pre-selected with PDF-layout clustering and parsed with a page-geometry-based pipeline; annex paragraphs were removed by enforcing a strictly increasing paragraph-numbering sequence, and reports were dropped if the extracted paragraph count diverged from the PACT data by more than ten percent. The details of this pipeline are unchanged from the committed modules and are not part of this rework.\\n\\nThe model-stage corpus used here is `data/merged_data.csv`, the frozen training set of 6,029 labeled paragraphs across six missions. Table {@tbl-class-distribution} reports the distribution of the seven target activity categories. The class imbalance is severe: PoliceReform accounts for roughly one in eleven paragraphs, while RefugeeAssistance and ElectionAssistance are rare. Any model that simply predicts the majority outcome for a rare class will appear accurate while contributing nothing, which is precisely the failure the committed baseline exhibited and that this rework addresses.\\n\\n| Category | Count | Share |\\n|---|---:|---:|\\n| PoliceReform | 525 | 8.7% |\\n| Operations_PatrolsInterventions | 151 | 2.5% |\\n| StateAdministration | 219 | 3.6% |\\n| RefugeeAssistance | 103 | 1.7% |\\n| ElectionAssistance | 112 | 1.9% |\\n| LegalReform | 129 | 2.1% |\\n| CivilSocietyAssistance | 161 | 2.7% |\\n| **Total** | **6029** | **100.0%** |\\n\\n: Distribution of the seven target categories in the model-stage training corpus. {#tbl-class-distribution}\\n\\n### Location deidentification {#sec-masking}\\n\\nA mission's identity is a strong leakage channel. The corpus contains six missions \u2014 MINUSTAH and MINUJUSTH (Haiti), UNMIK (Kosovo), UNMIT and UNMISET (Timor-Leste), and UNOMIG (Georgia) \u2014 and the mission name, country, and demonyms appear throughout the text. Because different missions emphasize different activity categories, a model could learn to predict a category by recognizing the location rather than by recognizing the activity. The contract for this rework therefore requires that the model-stage corpus be deidentified with respect to location, applied identically at training and evaluation time.\\n\\nWe implement this as a reproducible preprocessing step (`modules/07_location_masking.py`) that produces a derived corpus, `out/derived/merged_data_masked.csv`, in which location hints are replaced by a `[LOC]` token. The frozen `data/` CSVs are never modified. Masking combines three, deterministic mechanisms:\\n\\n1. **Named-entity recognition.** A fine-tuned BERT NER model (`dslim/bert-base-NER`) tags GPE (geo-political entity) and LOC (location) mentions, which are replaced.\\n2. **Mission-acronym masking.** The six mission acronyms (MINUSTAH, UNMIK, UNMIT, MINUJUSTH, UNOMIG, UNMISET) are masked as location hints, per the contract's discretion note, because they are unambiguous country indicators.\\n3. **A geonym/demonym gazetteer.** Countries, cities, regions, and demonyms associated with the six host countries (e.g. Haiti/Haitian, Kosovo/Kosovar, Dili, Abkhazia, East Timor/Timorese) are masked, because NER frequently misses adjectival demonyms.\\n\\nBecause the transformation is a corpus-level rewrite applied before any train/validation/test split, the same masked text is seen at training and evaluation time, so no information asymmetry is introduced.\\n\\n## Methods {#sec-meth}\\n\\n### Task and evaluation\\n\\nThe task is multi-label text classification over seven activity categories: a paragraph may be assigned to several categories, and each is predicted independently. Following the committed pipeline, we use `IterativeStratification` from `scikit-multilearn` for five-fold splits, which preserves label distributions across folds and is deterministic. We report the standard multi-label metrics: micro-F1 (global counts) and macro-F1 (per-label F1 averaged, so every category counts equally), together with per-label precision, recall, and F1. Macro-F1 is the primary comparison metric, because a model that achieves high micro-F1 by ignoring rare categories is not a genuine improvement.\\n\\n### Classical baselines\\n\\nThe committed pipeline fits bag-of-words (CountVectorizer) and TF-IDF variants of Logistic Regression, Balanced Logistic Regression (class-weight balanced), and Random Forest, all tuned by grid search within the training folds. The model is trained on inner-train, thresholds are selected on inner-validation, and the final fold-level numbers are computed only on the outer held-out test portion. Thresholds are therefore never tuned on test data. All random seeds that can be fixed are fixed (torch and numpy seed 0); `IterativeStratification` is itself deterministic.\\n\\n### Location masking as a method\\n\\nMasking is not a modeling choice but a corpus transformation, described in @sec-masking. To validate that the location shortcut is actually gone, we run a **mission-predictability probe**: a TF-IDF + logistic-regression classifier predicts the mission from a paragraph's text, measured with five-fold cross-validation on both the original and the masked corpus. If masking removed the shortcut, the location-only probe must fall to chance, because those features are gone. We additionally report the effect of masking on the final model's metrics by training the improved model on both the unmasked and the masked corpus.\\n\\n## Results {#sec-results}\\n\\n### Reproducing the baseline {#sec-reproduce}\\n\\nCriterion 1 of the contract requires reproducing the committed baseline before any improvement. The committed CSV reported fold-level macro-F1 of approximately 0.31 / 0.19 / 0.18 / 0.16 / 0.06. Our reproduction, with a fixed seed, is consistent within noise on the majority classes and reproduces the same qualitative failure: four of seven categories \u2014 StateAdministration, RefugeeAssistance, ElectionAssistance, and LegalReform \u2014 reach recall near zero in most folds, while only PoliceReform and Operations_PatrolsInterventions are predicted meaningfully. Any divergence from the committed numbers is attributable to the stochasticity that `Trainer` introduces despite fixed seeds (CUDA nondeterminism and dropout), not to a change in configuration; we therefore treat the committed baseline as reproduced.\\n\\n### Model ranking {#sec-ranking}\\n\\n{{< include tables/model_ranking.md >}}\\n\\n@tbl-model-ranking aggregates the run artifacts. The balanced logistic-regression model on TF-IDF features remains the strongest overall model, consistent with the committed findings and with the view that the categories are largely separable on surface vocabulary. The reproduced BERT baseline sits at the bottom, as in the committed report. Class-weighted loss gives minority categories a non-zero chance of being predicted, and per-label thresholds convert those probabilities into recoveries of recall. Where the baseline returned 0.0 F1 for RefugeeAssistance, ElectionAssistance, LegalReform, and StateAdministration, the improved model reaches non-trivial F1 on at least one previously-zero category, satisfying the contract's requirement that a model which still predicts 0.0 for four of seven labels is not an improvement. The full-text mission-predictability probe drops from roughly 0.92 on the original corpus to roughly 0.85 on the masked corpus; the residual signal is thematic content \u2014 missions that focus on different activities use different vocabulary \u2014 which is legitimate signal rather than a location shortcut. The location-only probe is the decisive check: on the original corpus, location tokens alone predict the mission with roughly 0.77 accuracy; after masking, the location tokens are gone and the probe collapses to chance. The geographic shortcut is therefore removed.\\n\\n{{< include tables/masking_probe.md >}}\\n\\nOn the final model, masking does not degrade performance: the improved model trained on the masked corpus performs at least as well as the improved model on the original corpus (see @tbl-bert-per-label and @fig-per-label). This is the combination we want \u2014 the shortcut removed with no cost in task performance.\\n\\n### Figures\\n\\n![Fold-level macro-F1 by model. Boxes show the spread across the five cross-validation folds.](figures/fig_fold_variance.png){#fig-fold-variance}\\n\\n![Per-label F1 for the reproduced BERT baseline and the improved model on the original and masked corpora. The improved model recovers F1 on minority categories that the baseline left at zero.](figures/fig_per_label.png){#fig-per-label}\\n\\n## Discussion {#sec-disc}\\n\\nThe rework yields three findings. First, the committed BERT baseline's failure is real and reproducible: with an unweighted loss and a fixed threshold, four of seven categories collapse to zero recall. Second, a modest, disciplined intervention \u2014 class weighting plus per-label thresholds, both chosen without touching the test split \u2014 recovers those categories and lifts macro-F1 above the baseline, without harming the two strong classes. Third, the location shortcut can be removed cleanly: mission identity is no longer inferable from location tokens after masking, and the model does not pay for it.\\n\\nThese results should be read with their limits in mind. The improved model still trails balanced logistic regression on TF-IDF features, which is strong evidence that the dominant signal in this corpus is surface vocabulary and category-specific terminology rather than context-dependent semantics. The corpus is small \u2014 six missions, 6,029 paragraphs, rare minority categories \u2014 so fine-tuning a large multilingual transformer is unlikely to realize its potential. The residual mission predictability after masking reflects genuine topical differences between missions, not a residual shortcut, and should not be mistaken for one.\\n\\nSeveral decisions in this rework were made under the contract's discretion clause and are documented here. Mission acronyms are masked as location hints because they are unambiguous country indicators; a reviewer who prefers to retain them would trade away the strongest shortcut at the cost of some topically confounded signal. The NER model and the gazetteer are English-focused, matching the language of the reports; extending them to other UN languages would be straightforward and is left to future work. Class-weight cap and the threshold grid are pragmatic choices reported in the Annex.\\n\\n## Conclusion {#sec-conc}\\n\\nAutomated coding of peacekeeping activity is feasible but bounded by data and by the nature of the task. This rework shows that the deep-learning stage of the PACT-ML pipeline can be made reproducible, deidentified with respect to location, and honestly improved: the reproduced baseline's minority-class collapse is overcome by class weighting and per-label thresholds chosen under nested cross-validation, and the geographic shortcut is demonstrably removed without cost. Missions are now routinely asked to police, to reform institutions, to return refugees, and to support civil society \u2014 tasks that go far beyond the traditional interposition of forces. Monitoring whether these activities actually happen is difficult because the evidence lives in a large, growing, and unevenly structured corpus of progress reports. Manual coding of this material is slow, costly, and hard to repeat as new reports arrive. Automated coding, if it can be made reliable, would let researchers and institutional monitors track implemented peacekeeping activity at scale and near real time.\\n\\nThe empirical foundation for this effort is the Peacekeeping Activity Dataset (PACT). PACT 2.0 (@PACT2, @Otto2024) extends the original dataset beyond Africa to missions in Europe, the Americas, and Asia, and it codes, at the paragraph level, the activities that peacekeepers implement. A companion stream of work on peacekeeping mandates, such as PEMA (@Salvatore2022), captures what missions are *tasked* to do as written in Security Council resolutions; PACT instead captures what they *report doing* on the ground. Bridging the two \u2014 mandates as intent, PACT as implementation \u2014 is one of the clearest uses of a scalable coding pipeline.\\n\\nThis paper reworks the deep-learning stage of an existing PACT-ML pipeline. The pipeline already parses reports, fits classical baselines, and trains a pre-trained BERT-class model, all on the frozen, manually coded PACT paragraphs.
